title: Tariff Refund Liquidation-Cliff Radar
one_liner: A deadline tracker and filing generator for small importers and small customs brokers that tells them, entry by entry, which refund route is still open and when it closes.
customer: Importers with 200-20,000 entries per year, and independent customs brokers serving them, who lack in-house trade counsel. Priced per entry or as a success fee.
problem: CBP will not refund automatically. Filers must act through CAPE, a Post Summary Correction (PSC) or a protest, and each route has a different window. CAPE Phase 1 accepts only unliquidated entries or entries liquidated in the preceding 80 days. Protests must be filed within 180 days of liquidation. PSCs must be filed within 300 days of entry or 15 days before liquidation. Finally liquidated entries, drawback, TIB and reconciliation entries are ineligible. The importer also needs ACE Portal access and ACH enrollment on file. Any outstanding CBP debt is offset first under 19 CFR 24.72.
solution: The tool ingests the ACE entry summary and liquidation reports (ES-003 or ES-022 exports, or a broker CSV). It assigns every IEEPA-duty entry a status and route (CAPE-eligible now, protest-only, PSC window, ineligible) and a hard 'last day' date. It auto-builds CAPE declaration files (up to 9,999 entries) for the broker and protest packets for the rest. It reconciles ACH deposits and interest against the ACE refund reports (REV-603 and REV-615) so the finance team can book the refund entry by entry. It flags CBP-debt offsets and scam solicitations, since CBP has warned about fraudsters targeting refund claimants.
why_now: The rolling cliff is live. Every month another vintage of 2025 entries liquidates, and each has a fresh 80-day CAPE window and a 180-day protest window that can lapse silently. Refunds are being recognised in one lump. AutoZone's alone was worth $4.43 EPS in a quarter. Auditors will require entry-level tie-outs.
revenue_model: $3-8 per entry tracked, $25K-$75K annual site licences for small brokers with 50+ importer clients, or a 3-5% success fee on refunds recovered from entries that would otherwise have gone finally liquidated.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a calendar, not law-firm expertise. CBP's own pages say 'ACE accepts CAPE Declarations containing entries liquidated within the preceding 80 days', 'once an entry has liquidated, a protest may be filed within 180 days', and 'you cannot remove entries from the Declaration' once filed (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds and https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/IEEPA-FAQ). CBP says only the IOR or its broker can file, and the FAQ never mentions automatic refunds. Public companies are already booking eight-figure refunds (AutoZone about $96M, MillerKnoll $16.5M, Worthington $4M: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/worthington-wor-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). The long tail of small importers is running on broker email chains and is the most likely to lose entries to a missed window.
first_30_days: Cold-email and call 100 independent customs brokers (from NCBFAA and local port broker lists) with an offer: 'send us your entry list and we'll return a route-and-deadline sheet within 24 hours, free'. Build the classifier in a spreadsheet plus a Python script. Publish a public liquidation-date calculator as a lead magnet aimed at importers. Convert the first 3 brokers to a paid per-entry contract, and have each refer 5-10 importer clients.

title: Paid Farm Residencies That Recruit Successors
one_liner: Multi-week hospitality-designed farm stays that let heir-less owners audition would-be farmers, monetising the stay and taking a success fee if a lease-to-own follows.
customer: Owners aged 65+ of orchards, vineyards, dairies and livestock farms with no heir, plus career-changing or remote-working would-be farmers with capital who pay for the residency. Farm Credit lenders and estate lawyers are referral partners.
problem: About one-third of US farmers have no obvious heir, and only about 1 in 4 has a formal succession plan. Over 60% of farmland may change hands in 10-15 years, much of it through estates that listing sites never see. Existing matching programs are listing databases, so skill and personal fit stay unresolved until people actually work together, and farm incomes are squeezed by input costs.
solution: Run 2-4 week residencies at $3K-$6K per guest with lodging, meals, remote-work setup (Starlink and a desk), and structured farm-management workshops on finances, equipment and land tenure. A shortlisted guest can take a paid trial season as a W-2 employee. Provide lender introductions (beginning-farmer loans) and lease-to-own and Buy-Protect-Sell templates, and take a success fee at transition. Winter orchard and vineyard pruning gives a bookable season within six months.
why_now: Remote work and nomad visas created the first cohort able to relocate to a farm without quitting a job. Bankruptcies up 19% and a fourth straight year of row-crop losses are pushing owners to plan exits, and the 'invisible transfer' wave means estates, not listings, decide who gets land. AI-assistant booking now lets tiny hosts sell stays directly.
revenue_model: Guest fees of $3K-$6K. A $750 farmer onboarding fee. A success fee of $15K-$25K or 1-2% of land or lease value at transition.
non_obvious_insight: Successors are not found in databases but in the third week of living together, so hospitality is the screening technology. The stay revenue pays the retiring farmer to audition candidates instead of paying a broker, and the trust built also unlocks the seller-financing that beginning farmers usually lack.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 specialty farms with owners aged 65+ in the Hudson Valley, Vermont, the Willamette Valley and Michigan. Open applications through career-change and nomad newsletters, and pre-sell 20 winter-pruning residencies for Dec-Mar.

title: Worker-Ownership Succession for Home Care Agencies
one_liner: A specialist shop that helps retiring home-care agency owners sell to their caregivers via an ESOP or worker co-op, plus a shared back office for the converted agencies.
customer: Owners aged 58-72 of $2-15M revenue home-care agencies with no successor. CDFI lenders and employee-ownership funds are financing partners.
problem: Reimbursement is squeezed (a 1.3% aggregate cut for CY2026, with a -3.0% temporary adjustment still in place), private-equity money goes to software and big platforms, and even UnitedHealth had to divest 164 Amedisys locations. Small owners have no buyer, while agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year.
solution: A conversion shop: valuation, readiness (licensure and payer change-of-ownership rules), structure (S-corp ESOP, worker co-op or employee-ownership trust), financing (seller note plus CDFI or SBA), and a two-year ownership-culture program (caregiver equity, profit sharing, scheduling voice). Converted agencies share a back office (payroll, billing, EVV, recruiting).
why_now: Boomer owners are retiring into a weak sales market after the 2026 rate squeeze, and the workforce shortage means the workforce is the scarcest asset. Cooperative Home Care Associates in the Bronx shows the model works.
revenue_model: Transaction fee of 3-5% of deal value, $8-15k a month back-office fees, and a small share of network EBITDA.
non_obvious_insight: In a business where turnover is the profit killer, the best buyer for a struggling agency is the workforce itself. Ownership is a retention tool, and the exit-plan angle sells to owners who don't care about culture.
first_30_days: Work with a state home-care association to get 20 owner conversations. Sell five $12k ownership-readiness assessments, line up a CDFI lender, and target first LOI within six months.

title: Keep-the-House Buyout Desk for Divorcing Spouses
one_liner: A divorce-specific mortgage desk that keeps the low-rate first mortgage alive, gets the leaving spouse released, and funds the equity buyout with a small second lien instead of a full high-rate cash-out refinance.
customer: Divorcing homeowners, mostly aged 40 to 65, who want to keep the house. Channels: mediators, divorce attorneys, CDFAs and DIY-divorce platforms.
problem: A divorce decree cannot release a co-borrower from the mortgage. Only a formal assumption with release, which requires servicer underwriting of the keeping spouse, or a refinance can do that. Many conventional loans are not assumable, though a transfer to a spouse under a decree is exempt from due-on-sale, while FHA, VA and USDA loans can be assumed. Servicers often mishandle these requests. Many homeowners hold first mortgages far below today's rates, so a full refinance wrecks affordability and the house gets sold.
solution: Intake on loan type, rate, equity and incomes, then a one-page keep versus sell versus refinance model showing blended-rate math. Then execute the sequence: title transfer under the divorce exemption, an assumption-with-release packet built for the servicer, buyout financing through a partner HELOC or closed-end second lien (or a shared-equity note from the leaving spouse), and suggested decree language for attorneys, such as a buyout-financing contingency and a release deadline.
why_now: Millions of borrowers still hold sub-4% mortgages while current rates are higher, and tappable home equity is large. The share of divorces involving people over 50 keeps growing, and those couples have the most equity. DIY-divorce platforms now produce decrees with no mortgage plan.
revenue_model: A flat $495 to $995 planning fee. Broker compensation of about 1% to 2% on second-lien or HELOC originations (requires an NMLS-licensed loan officer or partner). Licensing to DIY-divorce platforms and mediation firms. Avoid referral fees to attorneys because of fee-splitting rules.
non_obvious_insight: Lawyers treat the house as a property-division problem when it is a loan-portability problem. The low-rate first mortgage is often the most valuable asset in the marriage. Illustratively, keeping $300k at 3% and borrowing $100k at 8.5% blends to about 4.4%, versus about 6.5% on a $400k cash-out refinance, roughly $300 to $400 a month less in payment. Nobody in the divorce process is paid to run that comparison.
first_30_days: Partner with one NMLS-licensed loan officer and two HELOC or second-lien lenders. Publish the calculator and a 'divorce and your mortgage' guide. Offer 5 mediators, divorce attorneys or CDFAs a free house model for their next 10 clients. Process 5 live cases and build servicer-by-servicer playbooks on assumption timelines and release requirements. Then sell the flat-fee plan to DIY-divorce customers.

title: Scan-Before-Buyout: Digital Memory and Game Assets
angle: Pairing 1: Climate adaptation x Gaming/entertainment/live experiences/fandoms
one_liner: Capture homes and streets in flood buyouts and burn zones in game-engine-grade 3D before demolition. The program pays for compliance and memorial; asset licensing to games and film is upside.
customer: County and state hazard-mitigation offices running buyouts, their historic-preservation consultants, and community foundations or long-term recovery groups funding memorials. Secondary buyers are game studios, VFX houses and XR training vendors.
problem: Buyouts demolish hundreds of 50-year-old homes. Federal funding triggers historic-property review, and the mitigation is often recorded documentation costing thousands per structure and producing a binder nobody opens. Families lose the physical record of their home and street, and the neighborhood dissolves undocumented. Only about 13% of affected Palisades owners have started rebuilding, so many lots sit for years. Game and film studios pay for authentic real-world environments that are hard to source.
solution: A crew of ex-game and VFX 3D artists uses Gaussian-splat or photogrammetry capture to scan exteriors, streetscapes and, with owner consent, interiors in an afternoon per home. Deliverables: (a) a compliance-grade documentation package, (b) a walkable keepsake file for each family, and (c) a de-identified 'American small-town' building kit licensed to studios, with revenue share to the community memorial fund.
why_now: Post-2024/25 flood buyouts are reaching demolition, and BRIC's $1B was reinstated in March 2026. Capture cost collapsed with splatting tools and phone-grade scanning. Game and VFX layoffs put skilled 3D artists on the market (Ubisoft headcount fell from 18,666 to 16,590 and EA's new owners plan AI-driven cost cuts), while studios need cheaper environment art.
revenue_model: Government or foundation contracts of $1,500-4,000 per structure or $40-150K per neighborhood, an optional $49 family keepsake often paid by a recovery fund, and five-figure per-studio licenses for the asset kit with revenue share to the county.
non_obvious_insight: The compliance mandate pays the bills, not the games market. Creative-industry tooling makes a documentation chore that nobody enjoys far cheaper, and turns it into a bereavement product and a licensable asset library. The county gets a better deliverable and a revenue share instead of a cost center.
first_30_days: Offer a free pilot street of 10 homes to a buyout manager in a post-flood region (western North Carolina or the Texas Hill Country). Collect owner releases. Deliver the splats plus a template mitigation stipulation a state preservation office can accept. Sell an anonymized kit on Fab, Sketchfab or the Unity store to test demand. Pitch consulting firms for subcontract work and a community foundation for the memorial grant.

title: Shared Certified Operators for Tiny Water Systems
one_liner: A marketplace pairing retired and semi-retired certified water operators with mobile-home parks, small towns and rural systems that must legally have one and cannot hire one.
customer: Mobile-home parks, towns under 3,300 people, rural water districts, and schools, campgrounds and churches on their own wells. They pay $600 to $2,500 a month per system. Supply side: retired plant operators, and operators laid off by consolidations.
problem: Regulations require a state-certified operator in responsible charge. Roughly 30% to 50% of the workforce is retiring within a decade, small systems cannot offer a full-time salary, and losing the operator means violations, fines and boil notices. New lead and PFAS monitoring adds workload.
solution: Vet and license-match operators state by state, pair each with a cluster of 8 to 12 nearby systems, and run telemetry-based oversight (cheap chlorine-residual, tank-level and pump-current sensors) so the certified person supervises remotely while a local non-certified lead hand does routine tasks. The platform handles state contract-operator paperwork, liability insurance, scheduling and compliance reporting.
why_now: Retirements are hitting small systems hardest. Cheap LTE-M and satellite-capable water sensors make remote supervision affordable. Public SDWIS violation data provides a ready-made, ranked lead list.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer per system with the platform keeping 25% to 35%. Sensor kit resale or lease at about $1,500. Insurance and compliance-reporting add-ons. Later: state programs paying to reduce violations.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not labor hours; it is the legal signature of a certified operator. One operator with telemetry can responsibly oversee ten tiny systems, and the regulator's own violations database is the sales list.
first_30_days: Pull SDWIS operator-certification and monitoring violations for one state. Recruit 3 retired operators via the state operator association. Sign 3 to 5 mobile-home parks at about $750 a month with compliant contract-operator letters and install a $1.5k telemetry kit.

title: Pooled Buyer Mandates for Group Discounts
one_liner: Thousands of buyer agents sign standing purchase mandates ('I will pay up to $X if 200 others join') and vendors bid to fill the pooled demand.
customer: Startups and SMBs (10-200 employees) buying SaaS and business services (renewals, business insurance, telecom). Buyers pay a success fee and vendors pay for pre-committed demand.
problem: Small buyers lack bargaining power and time, and group purchasing organizations serve hospitals and enterprises, not the long tail. Vendors offer volume discounts against committed volume they cannot see. Agent payment standards now include signed intent mandates (Google's AP2, Mastercard's Verifiable Intent) that capture limits and constraints, and AP2 explicitly anticipates group scenarios, yet no product pools them.
solution: A mandate pool where each buyer or their agent signs an intent mandate with price ceiling, term and threshold. The exchange aggregates by category, shows vendors a live demand curve with reservation prices, and runs a sealed-bid reverse auction when the threshold is met. Purchases execute through each buyer's own payment mandate. First category: annual SaaS renewals, a Vendr for the long tail.
why_now: AP2 (September 2025), Verifiable Intent and UCP provide the first standard way to hold cryptographically signed, pre-authorized purchase intent. Agents now run procurement tasks, and vendors moving to agent meters want volume signals.
revenue_model: 5-10% of buyer savings or a 2-4% vendor fee on pooled transactions.
non_obvious_insight: A signed intent is a binding, machine-readable limit order for goods, so small buyers can pre-commit credibly without a human negotiating. That credibility is what makes group buying scale, like Kickstarter for procurement.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 startups from a founder community to pledge to 5 popular tools through a web form (protocol integration later). Bring the demand curve to 5 vendors and close one pooled deal to prove price.

title: Universal Robot Cone: Vendor-Neutral Keep-Out Zones
one_liner: One tap, or one cheap beacon dropped on the floor, creates a temporary no-go zone that every robot brand in the building obeys, with a log to prove it.
customer: 3PL and warehouse operators and hospital operations teams running multi-vendor AMRs, AGVs and autonomous scrubbers or forklifts, especially their safety managers and insurers.
problem: Mixed fleets each have their own fleet manager and zone tool. A worker who finds a spill, opens a lift or spots a person in an aisle cannot instantly stop every robot across vendors. E-stops are vendor-specific and incident evidence is fragmented. Existing standards cover fleet control (VDA 5050) or monitoring (MassRobotics), but neither provides a neutral, human-triggered safety boundary.
solution: Phase 1 is software: a tablet or wearable app that pushes a temporary keep-out polygon, with expiry and audit, to each vendor's fleet-manager API at once. Phase 2 is a $60-100 BLE/UWB and visual-marker beacon 'cone' that creates dynamic zones, with an open spec pitched to standards bodies. A neutral log records who created and cleared each zone and which robots entered it.
why_now: Multi-vendor fleets, many imported, are now normal in large warehouses and insurers say they are unprepared. VDA 5050 and MassRobotics adapters make cross-vendor integration feasible. ISO 3691-4 audits and rising incident claims give safety managers budget.
revenue_model: $300-800 per site per month for the software, about $75 per beacon, integration or certification fees from robot OEMs who want 'cone-compatible' status, and possible insurer premium discounts shared with customers.
non_obvious_insight: The safety stop line is the one thing every vendor must honor and the one thing no vendor wants to own across competitors. Whoever owns the neutral stop line owns the cross-vendor safety log, which becomes the reference record in any liability dispute.
first_30_days: Visit 10 warehouses running two or more robot vendors. Build adapters for two or three fleet APIs with open documentation. Run a paid pilot with one 3PL at $500 per month, used in a safety drill. Ask the site's broker for an endorsement letter.

title: Abandoned Property and Tenant-Death Response Crew
one_liner: A per-event service that handles the legally dangerous moments landlords dread most, such as a tenant who vanishes leaving belongings or a tenant who dies alone, with statutory clocks, next-of-kin outreach and documented disposal.
customer: Property managers and small landlords, who pay per event ($400 to $1,500). Later customers are eldercare social workers, hospital discharge teams, medical examiners' offices and estate attorneys, who all need someone to close out a residence properly.
problem: A 400-unit manager deals with a handful of abandonments a year and one to three tenant deaths. Each event is handled ad hoc. Abandoned-property statutes vary by state, with notice periods, itemized inventory rules, value thresholds and sale-or-storage requirements. One mistake, such as tossing a bin or entering too early, creates conversion or wrongful-eviction liability. With a death, no one has authority to enter or dispose of belongings, the estate has no representative yet, next of kin are unknown or hostile, rent accrues, and the unit sits dark for months. Hoarding and biohazard situations make it worse. There is no standard vendor, so the maintenance supervisor is doing legal and emotional work no one trained him for.
solution: A regional response team with a state-specific statutory workflow. Step one is intake and legal-clock software, which starts the required notice dates, produces the notices, photo-inventory and valuation report and stores it as evidence. Step two is next-of-kin and estate-representative outreach, with sensitivity training for the caller. Step three is secure storage in a partner facility, then sale, donation or disposal exactly as the statute allows, with receipts. Step four is coordinating hoarding or biohazard remediation and the final walk-through for deposit accounting. A companion product is an e-signable lease addendum letting tenants (especially seniors) name an emergency contact and authorized person for post-death property disposition, in the states where that is permitted. That builds a pipeline of pre-authorized cases and makes each later event simple.
why_now: The number of renters aged 65+ living alone is growing fast, which means more deaths in rental units and more hoarding and welfare issues. Several states have recently added or modernized tenant-designated-contact and abandoned-property procedures, though rules remain patchy. Software-only proptech has ignored this because it is field work. Junk-removal and storage marketplaces have made the physical logistics cheap to subcontract.
revenue_model: $400 to $1,500 flat fee per abandonment or death event, plus pass-through storage and disposal cost at a 15 to 25% markup. Optional readiness subscription ($1 to $2 per unit per month) for PMs, covering the lease addendum, templates and priority response. Eldercare and estate-attorney referral relationships add a second channel.
non_obvious_insight: Ordinary landlords fear the eviction. Experienced managers fear the abandonment and the death, because the law in those cases punishes shortcuts, no procedure exists, and the loss (months of rent plus liability) is bigger than a normal eviction. Nobody sells the service because each case is small and the required knowledge is a stack of 50 state statutes. That fragmentation is the moat: once you have playbooks for a handful of states, competitors cannot copy them quickly.
first_30_days: Pick one state and read the abandoned-property and death-of-tenant statutes closely, ideally with a landlord-tenant attorney on a fixed-fee review. Build the notice, inventory and timeline templates. Sign three PMs (find them through the local NARPM or apartment association) to a pilot: 'call us on the next event, first one at cost'. Line up a junk-removal company, a storage unit partner and a biohazard remediation subcontractor. Publish a simple blog page and a landlord-association talk titled 'What to do when a tenant dies or disappears' to start inbound.

title: Silver Crews: Retiree Work Co-ops for US Towns
one_liner: A membership co-op for retirees 62+ that contracts with towns, school districts and HOAs for short, insured, daytime jobs (crossing guards, school and library aides, grounds work, event staffing) and acts as employer of record.
customer: Municipal public-works and parks departments, school districts, libraries, HOAs and property managers who pay per job-hour. Retirees join as members.
problem: Employers with 5-15 hour-a-week daytime needs can't hire for them. Retirees want flexible, meaningful part-time work but distrust app gigs and can't easily get liability and accident cover. A record 4.18M Americans turned 65 in 2025, crossing guards are already the most senior-dominated occupation (nearly 1 in 3 are 65+), and about 15% of retirees say they'd consider returning to paid work.
solution: A county-level 'Silver Crew' modeled on Japan's Silver Human Resource Centers (about 1,300 centers, 700,000+ members). It recruits, background-checks and trains 200-400 members, holds standing contracts, schedules shifts, runs payroll (W-2 or contract), carries pooled workers'-comp/accident insurance, and hosts a monthly social meetup. Customers get a reliable pool without hiring headaches, and members get a community as well as a paycheck.
why_now: Peak 65 will stay elevated through at least 2027, school and municipal labor shortages persist, and municipal budgets favor contracting over adding headcount. Japan's centers have proven the model over decades, while US equivalents are small nonprofit senior-employment programs, not service-contract businesses.
revenue_model: Mark-up of roughly 15-25% on member pay billed to customers, small annual member dues, and margin on pooled insurance.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input isn't retiree labor, it's the wrapper. A town can't onboard a 68-year-old for six hours a week, but a co-op with pooled accident cover, one background-check process and a single invoice can. Japanese centers work because the arrangement is legally a contract for a task, not a job, which strips out friction. The social meetup is the retention engine, and it is what makes seniors choose this over Uber or DoorDash.
first_30_days: Pick one retiree-dense county (Florida, Arizona or a New England town). Sign 3 pilot contracts (an HOA, a school district and a library) using an existing PEO for payroll and workers' comp. Recruit 40 retirees through senior centers, churches and Nextdoor. Run the first paid shifts within 4 weeks and invoice monthly.

title: Layoff Compliance Autopilot for Mid-Size HR
one_liner: Software plus expert review that generates every notice, filing and adverse-impact analysis a reduction-in-force needs, including a documented record of whether AI or restructuring drove each decision.
customer: HR and legal teams at 200-5,000-employee companies and the boutique employment law firms advising them pay $4-15k per event or $12-30k a year.
problem: RIF rules are fragmenting by state. New York's WARN form asks whether layoffs stem from AI or automation, New Jersey mandates severance, and OWBPA requires age disclosures for group terminations. Remote workforces span 20+ states. Mid-size firms rely on $500-an-hour outside counsel or spreadsheets while age-bias and AI-washing scrutiny (Mobley v. Workday) rises.
solution: Upload the roster and selection criteria. The tool maps each jurisdiction's rules, generates notices, separation agreements and OWBPA disclosures, runs adverse-impact statistics (age, race, sex, disability, leave) with remediation suggestions, and builds an AI-attribution record of task-level evidence for each decision. It includes a filing calendar and a lawyer-in-the-loop review queue.
why_now: Cuts are steady even though Challenger totals are down 41% year on year, AI is the leading cited reason, and NY added an AI checkbox in 2025. Age-discrimination class actions are live, and LLMs now make document generation cheap while lawyers still sign off.
revenue_model: Per-event fee ($4-15k), annual subscription, and revenue share with reselling law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The pain is not 'AI layoffs' but the compliance combinatorics of remote-first firms. The economic buyers (law firms and HR) either bill by the hour or bear the risk, and steady low-volume cuts mean repeated use.
first_30_days: Build a state-by-state rule matrix for the top 12 states plus federal rules. Sell $2,500 'RIF readiness packs' to 10 boutique employment firms. Run three live RIF events with friendly firms.

title: Loss-Draft Concierge for Disaster Rebuilds
one_liner: A draw desk that gets the insurance money for a destroyed house out of the mortgage servicer's restricted account and into the rebuild, paid by the contractors who need cash to start.
customer: Mortgaged homeowners whose houses were destroyed or damaged by fire, flood or storm pay $1,500-3,000 flat or about 1% of proceeds. Rebuild contractors pay 1.5-2.5% of each accelerated draw.
problem: When a mortgaged house is destroyed, insurance checks are made out to both the owner and the servicer. The servicer parks the money in a loss-draft account and releases it in inspection-gated stages, each requiring a contract, contractor license proof, permits, lien waivers, W-9s and photos. Homeowners cannot assemble the packet. Contractors will not start without money. Families pay rent and a mortgage on a lot with nothing on it. Rebuild fraud thrives in the gap.
solution: A draw desk that takes the servicer's letter and builds the draw packet in the exact format the servicer wants. It verifies the contractor's license, collects conditional and unconditional lien waivers on the state statutory forms, books inspections, submits, and chases weekly. It escalates to servicer executive complaint lines and state regulators. It ties every disbursement to milestone photos and waivers so the homeowner is protected from paying for work not done. It never holds the funds, which avoids money-transmitter issues. Later add bridge financing against expected draws.
why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures and rebuilds are now at peak permit and construction paperwork. Storm and flood rebuilds continue in Texas, North Carolina and Florida, and every season adds more. Additional-living-expense coverage has clocks that expire, which makes delay costly. AI document handling makes lien-waiver, permit and inspection-photo checks cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: Flat rebuild-admin package or about 1% of proceeds from homeowners. A per-draw acceleration fee of 1.5-2.5% from contractors. Later, a spread on bridge loans and referral revenue from lenders and builders.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not the insurer. The money already exists and is locked behind paperwork the homeowner cannot produce. Public adjusters take about 10% to fight the insurer but nobody specializes in this second fight. The hidden buyer is the contractor, whose cash flow decides whether the site ever starts.
first_30_days: Join fire-survivor community groups and rebuild nonprofits in one affected area. Offer a free draw-packet review to the first 10 households. Sign 3 rebuild contractors whose draws are stalled. Charge a flat fee only after the first draw is released. Document days-to-funds before and after as your proof, then take the case studies to the next disaster market.

title: Drive-By Lawsuit Shield for Marketing Stacks
one_liner: Scan and fix the text, website and review flows that trigger serial-plaintiff demand letters, and back it with a response pack.
customer: Local-service SMBs and small multi-location brands, sold mostly through local marketing agencies and agency resellers on GoHighLevel, Wix and Squarespace.
problem: Serial-plaintiff waves target small firms: text-message consent and quiet-hours claims, website accessibility claims, wiretap claims over chat widgets and tracking pixels, and the FTC's fake-and-gated-review rule (prior knowledge on the rules). Demands of $5-25k get settled blind. AI-generated marketing raises exposure: 83% of AI-using small firms use AI for writing or marketing.
solution: A scanner checks known triggers: SMS consent capture and state quiet hours, trackers and chat widgets without consent banners, basic accessibility failures, review-gating flows and unsubstantiated claims. It applies or guides fixes, keeps a provenance-stamped consent ledger, and provides a demand-letter response pack via a partner law firm. Defense-cost coverage can be added through an MGA.
why_now: SMBs are now running automated texting, AI-written content and review requests, and small businesses lack legal capacity to evaluate demands.
revenue_model: $19-49 per site or number per month, $499 per response pack, plus a share of insurance premiums.
non_obvious_insight: The vendor who sells the marketing tool never gets sued, but the owner does, and the agency is liable to its client. The buyer of protection is the agency reseller, not the owner.
first_30_days: Build scanners for three triggers and run free scans on 500 local sites. Sell reports to 10 agencies and sign a law-firm partner for the response pack.

title: Pre-Permitted School Suites for Micro-Schools
angle: Pairing 2: Real estate (vacant office, change-of-use) x Gen Alpha, AI-native education
one_liner: Master-lease vacant office and retail suites, pre-solve the change-of-use to educational occupancy, and rent furnished seats by the student to micro-school operators funded by education savings accounts.
customer: Micro-school networks and guides (per-student monthly seat rent), landlords of vacant suites (a paying tenant with no build-out risk), and ESA-funded parents underneath.
problem: Universal ESAs are minting demand: Texas alone funds $10,474 per student for 2026-27, drew 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks, and micro-school networks like Primer are opening campuses to serve it. The gate is the certificate of occupancy, not curriculum or demand. More than five children generally triggers Group E in the building code, and founders discover egress, restroom count, fire alarm and ADA gaps after signing a lease. Landlords have no standard lease and fear liability. AI-guided micro-schools need only about 25-40 sq ft per student and a few hours of adaptive software.
solution: A master-lessee that holds a portfolio of pre-engineered suites (ground floor, existing restrooms, former daycare, church, tutoring or medical use) with permit packages per jurisdiction. It subleases furnished seats month to month with a cancellation clause if ESA funding lapses, standard landlord-friendly leases and pooled insurance, plus an opening checklist and inspector relationships.
why_now: Texas ESAs go live in 2026-27 and the federal tax-credit scholarship program begins in 2027, on top of a dozen-plus states with existing ESAs. Office vacancy is 17.8%, maturity-wall landlords will take any creditworthy tenant, and the school-age population is shifting toward small-cohort, phone-light models.
revenue_model: Spread between master lease and per-seat rent (25-35% gross margin), TI financing fees, and a subscription for operators to use the permit-pack library.
non_obvious_insight: Micro-school growth is gated by a building department, not by families or teachers. The party that holds the permits, not the curriculum, owns the supply chain, and vacant offices are the wrong space until someone pre-solves the change of use.
first_30_days: Pick Texas (Austin, Dallas, Houston or San Antonio) and map 40 vacant suites with existing daycare or ground-floor restroom stock. Sign one or two 12-month master leases. Pre-sell three operators and open one site by January 2027 for spring enrollment. Get a code consultant to write a reusable permit checklist.

title: PFAS Farm Passport for Food Buyers and Lenders
one_liner: A screening-plus-sampling service that tells dairy co-ops, produce processors and ag lenders which supplier farms carry PFAS risk from sludge spreading or contaminated irrigation water, and certifies the clean ones.
customer: Dairy co-ops, regional produce and hay buyers, private-label sourcing teams and agricultural lenders. The buyer pays for its supplier base, and farms pay for re-verification.
problem: The industry frames PFAS as a 4 ppt tap-water rule, and EPA's proposed delay to 2031 and rescissions seem to give slack. The abrupt financial shock is on farms: biosolids-spread fields and PFAS-laden irrigation or well water (Maine's shut-down farms are the precedent). There is no farm-level limit, so lenders and buyers cannot underwrite.
solution: A 'PFAS Farm Passport'. First, a desktop risk screen from public biosolids-application permits, industrial discharger locations and nearby well data. Second, a targeted sampling protocol (irrigation water, soil, forage, milk) run through a partner lab. Third, a risk tier and a 'verified clean' attestation for buyers and lenders. Fourth, remediation triage (change water source, crop or field use).
why_now: Regulatory loosening pushes risk assessment onto private buyers, who cannot wait for rules. The 2027 monitoring data will make PFAS geography public. Maine-style farm closures have put buyers on notice, and private supplier standards tend to outrun public ones.
revenue_model: $300-800 desktop screen per farm (paid by buyer), $1-3k per sampling round, $100-300k/yr enterprise contracts for processors with 500-2,000 suppliers, and lender portfolio-screening fees.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers fear being caught selling contaminated milk, not violating a tap-water limit. In food supply chains a private standard beats the public rule, so the gap between the EPA rollback and buyer fear is the market.
first_30_days: Choose one region with open biosolids-application records (Michigan, Wisconsin or Maine). Screen 500 farms desktop-only. Give three regional dairy co-ops or processors a free 'top 20 at-risk suppliers' preview, and sell a paid 50-farm sampling pilot.

title: Parametric Outage Cover for Satellite Internet Users
one_liner: A $60 probe network and parametric policy that pays cash when a satellite-dependent operation loses connectivity.
customer: Mines, farms, offshore and maritime fleets, remote clinics and construction firms whose operations run on a single LEO link.
problem: Insiders treat Starlink as a utility. Operator SLAs give small credits, while the customer's loss is stopped production, idle crews or a stalled remote-operations center. Insurers avoid the risk because they have no independent measurement.
solution: Ship a probe that actively tests the customer's link and cross-checks against a global mesh of other probes. That produces tamper-resistant uptime evidence. Sell a parametric policy that pays a fixed amount per hour beyond a threshold, underwritten by an MGA and reinsurers. Add failover advice and an independent uptime scorecard for SLA negotiation.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, and enterprise, maritime and rural operations now depend on it. A widely reported global outage in July 2025 (prior knowledge) showed correlated failure is real. Amazon and others are launching alternatives to fail over to.
revenue_model: Probe subscription $30-100 per month per site. Premium about 4-8% of annual connectivity spend once the policy launches. Data licensing to reinsurers.
non_obvious_insight: Correlated single-vendor outages are actually easy to model, and the true blocker was measurement, not appetite. A cheap independent probe network converts an 'uninsurable' risk into a priced one.
first_30_days: Build the probe on a Raspberry Pi and deploy on 50 friendly terminals from RV, farm and maritime communities. Publish an uptime dashboard. Approach two MGAs about a pilot policy and sell probe subscriptions to three fleets.

title: Immune-Training Forest-Floor Yards for Daycares
one_liner: A certified installation and refill service that replaces sterile daycare yards with vetted forest floor and sod to diversify children's skin and gut microbiota.
customer: Private daycare chains, preschool operators, nature-based preschools and municipal early-childhood departments in cities, especially ones competing on parent trust and outdoor programming.
problem: Allergies, asthma and immune disorders are rising in urban kids, who spend 8+ hours a day in daycare yards of plastic, gravel and rubber mulch with almost no microbial diversity. Parents worry, but the options are vague 'nature play' features with no evidence of health impact.
solution: Biodiversity kits based on the Finnish protocol: about 100 m2 of pathogen-screened forest floor litter and 200 m2 of sod, planter boxes and simple play rules, sourced from vetted local woodland. We add a seasonal refill and an optional microbiome swab study, all under a 'Biodiversity Certified' badge that daycares can show to parents.
why_now: There is direct peer-reviewed evidence. In a study of 10 Finnish daycares with 75 children aged 3-5, adding forest floor and sod for 28 days changed skin and gut microbiota and immune markers (Roslund et al., Science Advances, 2020), and a 2021 follow-up on long-term effects was published. Parents are more microbiome-aware, and cities are funding cooling and greening of schoolyards.
revenue_model: One-time install of roughly $6-15k per yard plus an annual refill subscription of roughly $1-2k per year, since the biology decays and litter needs replacing. Licensing of the certification badge to chains, and public-tender revenue from cities.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody can patent dirt, so the moat is safe sourcing, pathogen testing and certification, and the recurring consumable makes it a regional supply chain of local ecological material. Selling 'immune infrastructure' to childcare works because the buyer's real problem is parent trust, and a visible, evidence-backed feature beats a marketing claim.
first_30_days: Contact 10 forest schools and one small chain. Build a 30 m2 pilot with a local soil scientist and a university microbiologist for about $1.5k. Set up a baseline and follow-up swab pilot and sell the first three paid yards to chains that want a differentiator.

title: Origin Assay: Forensic Testing of Metal Melt Origin
one_liner: A lab test that says where steel or aluminum was actually melted, so US-melt claims stop resting on paperwork alone.
customer: Importers and fabricators claiming the 10% US-melt rate, steel service centers selling premium 'US-melt' stock, customs counsel and insurers defending CBP audits, and buyers with domestic-metal requirements.
problem: Section 232 rates now depend on melt or smelt origin: 10% with US-melted metal against 25-50%. The certificate is worth thousands of dollars per ton, mill test reports can be relabeled or forged, and CBP is prioritizing origin verification and AD/CVD evasion. No independent test exists.
solution: Build a reference library by buying coupons from about 100 mills worldwide. Measure trace-element, inclusion and slag chemistry, and isotopic signatures (LIBS, ICP-MS, SEM-EDS). Train a classifier to give origin probability. First product is a mail-in Origin Assay with a confidence-scored report and sampling protocol built for audits. Handheld screening is a later roadmap. Classifier accuracy is the central risk, so start with one narrow discrimination, such as US EAF versus Chinese plate for one grade.
why_now: The 2026 tiers turn a chemistry fact into a financial asset. Cheaper mass spectrometry and machine learning make library-based classification plausible, and academic provenance work exists but no commercial library does (verify).
revenue_model: $300-900 per sample. $25-100k annual audit programs for service centers. Insurer verification programs. Later, handheld subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Duty policy turned melt origin into money, and paper certificates invite cheating, so the arbitrage is proof. Scrap-based EAF steel carries a fingerprint of tramp elements and alloy history that makes origin partly knowable.
first_30_days: Interview three service centers and three customs counsel. Buy or borrow about 40 heats of known origin (A36 and 304). Use a university ICP-MS lab to test discriminating power on two grades. Sell a $5k pilot verification of 10 suspicious heats.

title: Surety Bonds for Agent Operators
one_liner: A customs bond for bots: agent operators post a surety-backed bond so sites, APIs and merchants can say yes to their agents and get paid if the agents misbehave.
customer: Mid-size vendors of browser, shopping and procurement agents ($1M-$50M ARR) whose agents get blocked or throttled. They pay for the bond and credential. Merchants and API providers consume the signal for free.
problem: Agent identity schemes (signed agents, know-your-agent) say who an agent is, not who pays when it scrapes abusively, mis-buys or triggers chargebacks. Agents are cheap to recreate, so identity carries no cost of failure. Bots are now 57.4% of requests, so sites default to blocking. After the August 2026 Ninth Circuit Comet ruling, blocking has to rest on contract and technical measures, so sites need a concrete reason to let agents in.
solution: Underwrite the operator (KYB, behavior review, volume caps). Issue a surety or insurer-backed bond ($25k-$1M penal sum) plus a signed credential that plugs into existing agent-auth headers and protocols. Sites whitelist a bonded lane with higher rate limits. A small claims desk pays on signed request logs. Wedge: agent vendors selling into mid-market merchants and B2B API providers that would create a bonded lane in their bot rules.
why_now: Bots overtook humans in 2026, and the Ninth Circuit ruling shifts blocking to contract terms. Neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding agent-dispute rule, and Visa's merchant dispute threshold tightened to 1.5% in April 2026, so merchants are risk-averse. Bonding has been proposed only in academic papers so far, and no product exists.
revenue_model: Bond premium share (typically 1-3% of penal sum per year) plus a $500-$5,000/month underwriting and credential fee, plus surety agency commission.
non_obvious_insight: Trust that scales in commerce rests on bonds, not identity. Freight brokers, contractors and customs brokers all post bonds. A bond makes an operator's reputation costly to abandon, and a site only has to trust the surety, not the operator.
first_30_days: Partner with a small surety agency or MGA to draft a miscellaneous bond form and a claims evidence standard. Recruit 5 agent vendors that merchants block and 5 merchants or API providers willing to whitelist. Sell the first 3 pilot bonds at $500-$1,500 per year plus a setup fee.

title: Whisper Director for Immersive Theatre and LARP
one_liner: Beacon badges plus an AI conductor that whispers real-time cues to human actors so a 100-guest immersive show feels individually authored.
customer: Immersive theatre companies, escape-room chains, LARP organizers, corporate murder-mystery producers, and Meow Wolf-style venues.
problem: Immersive magic depends on actors responding to each guest, but no actor can track 100 people. Guests get generic loops, and shows stay small and unprofitable. Meow Wolf's Los Angeles and New York venues and Sphere's $420.5M gross show the demand.
solution: Version 1 is a stage-manager console. Guests wear BLE or UWB badges, software tracks paths and story flags, and an LLM plus rules engine produces cue whispers for performers via bone-conduction earpieces. There are no AI actors, only human performers with better information. Start with 40-person murder-mystery dinners and LARPs.
why_now: Low-latency LLMs and voice models, cheap beacons, and a live-experience boom make this feasible now, and the market is pushing toward permanent immersive venues.
revenue_model: $300-1,500 per production week, $5 per guest hardware rental, and licences for permanent installs.
non_obvious_insight: AI in entertainment is aimed at replacing performers, but the constrained resource in immersive theatre is coordination bandwidth, not talent. Human performers plus a conductor scales what audiences pay for.
first_30_days: Partner with 3 immersive producers or LARP groups. Rent BLE tags and run a 15-person cast pilot at a Halloween or winter event. Sell paid pilots at $2-4k per event.
